## Market Developments 

**Copper prices finished 2009 on a high** Overall official 3-month quotes averaged $5185/t in 2009, down by 25% from 2008’s average of $6883/t.  During December copper prices (3m) averaged $7017/t which was up by 4.7% on November ($6697/t) and represented the highest monthly figure for the year.  During the final months of 2009 prices were supported by supply disruptions resulting from a combination of industrial action and ongoing wage negotiations as well as by strong economic and demand growth in China.  These factors continued to be supportive during the first two weeks of January with prices having risen from $7376/t at the end of last year to $7698/t on the 11<sup>th</sup> , a new 17-month high. However, since the 12<sup>th</sup> official prices (3m) have come under downward pressure mainly from adverse news (emanating out of China) and are currently trading around $6900/t.  Despite this reduction, as of the 28<sup>th</sup> the month-to-date average of $7440/t is still an increase of 6% over last month’s average. 

**Industrial action now less supportive** During the first week of the January prices were supported by industrial action in Chile at Xstrata’s Altonorte smelter and Codelco’s large Chuquicamata copper mining and smelting complex.  Around 40% of the Altonorte workforce began strike action on December 28<sup>th</sup> after rejecting a collective wage agreement which was offered after five days of government-mediated talks.  Elsewhere at Chuquicamata, over 5000 workers walked out on January 4<sup>th</sup> after rejecting the company’s latest wage offer.  However, as is often the case in Chile both strikes proved to be short-lived with workers at the Chuquicamata complex returning to work two days later and the Altonorte walkout barely lasting a week.  Subsequently, news broke of wage settlements at Lumwana and Mopani in Zambia although several negotiations still remain unresolved (see PRODUCTION). 

**Chinese economic growth stronger than expected** The release of positive Chinese economic data during the second week of January was largely responsible for official 3-month quotes reaching their highest level since August 2008 on the 11<sup>th</sup> .  The data showed that Chinese economic growth had remained strong through the closing stages of 2009.  The country’s GDP increased by a higher than expected 10.7% in Q4 from the corresponding period in 2008.  For the year as a whole GDP rose by 8.7% which was above the government’s target of 8%.  Two of the main supportive factors were the (unsustainable) growth in lending and monetary stimuli. 

**China introduces tighter monetary controls** Nevertheless, the downside of the positive GDP figures was Chinese government concern that the economy was growing too quickly and may overheat.  Thus in mid-January the first measure in tightening monetary policy was introduced.  The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) increased its

Reserve Requirement Ration (RRR) by 0.5% to 16% which became effective on the 18th . This represented the first change in the reserve ration since December 2008. Such action dampened market sentiment as did growing concerns by market participants that the PBOC may introduce additional measures to slow Chinese economic growth. These two factors were largely responsible for official 3-month quotes following a downward trend from the 11th . **Volatile trading conditions persist** Increased volatility in trading conditions was very much in evidence this month with daily min/max variations in official 3-month quotes ranging from-$243/t to +$232/t as of the 28th . Fuelling this volatility has been a 180 degrees reversal in sentiment. On the upside, participants were initially encouraged by positive economic news emanating from China, the opening up of arbitrage trading between the SHFE and the LME and industrial action. However, sentiment has turned distinctly more bearish as the month has progressed on the back of monetary policy tightening in China, an appreciating US dollar and technical factors. ### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 280000 8000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2010 Page 2 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **LME open interest highlights market uncertainty** This change in market sentiment was highlighted by LME open interest data which is currently significantly lower than the levels seen in mid-December. The initial sharp decline in December is a perennial feature in open interest across the metals, as positions are closed out at year end. Following this decline open interest climbed in tandem with prices, carrying on the trend seen in H2 2009 of long position building. However, during the second half of January this situation reversed quite markedly with a wave of apparent long liquidation pushing prices lower. This data suggests that investors are now less certain about copper being a one-way bet as regards price direction, prompting a sell off in order to cash in their recent (and substantial) gains. **Exchange stocks continue to rise** Total exchange stocks increased for the seventh consecutive month in January, rising by a net 47.4kt to 736.2kt, as of the 28th . This is the first time since January 2004 that total exchange inventories have exceeded 700kt. In terms of days of consumption, total inventories are now 9.2 days. Furthermore, net increases were recorded on all three exchanges and this has not occurred since October 2009. SHFE inventories increased by a ne

t 4.8kt, to 101.2kt, and warrants in Comex warehouses rose by a net 3.9kt to 93.9kt. At the same time, LME stocks jumped by a net 38.7kt to 541.1kt, their highest level since September 2003. The majority of the increase in LME inventories reflected deliveries (32.1kt) into warehouses in the US, with New Orleans (+31.5kt) being the preferred location. The increase was not surprising given the ongoing sluggish demand for copper in the US. However, on a slightly positive note, cancelled warrants on the LME increased during the month. Cancelled warrants rose from 3.1kt at the end of December to 9.2kt, as of the 28th , with most (9.1kt) of the warrants were located in South Korea. This most likely reflects material destined for China, where arbitrage buying has picked up significantly during the month. **European spot premia levels improve** European premia have strengthened during the month despite meagre physical spot activity. We hear that the higher levels are more a reflection of the higher rates in China rather than any underlying pick up in demand in Europe. Codelco, for example, is apparently offering material into Europe at elevated levels solely on the back of higher premia in Shanghai. As a consequence, Chilean and Grade A warrants in Rotterdam are now trading between $80-90/t compared with $55/t in December. Elsewhere, Italian warrants in Livorno remained at $75/t while standard grade cathode quotes were also unchanged at $20/t. **Premia weaken in the US but firm in China** US premia weakened during the month, falling from 3.5c/lb in December to 3c/lb currently. At the same time, in areas where cathode has been plentiful, some consumers have been able to purchase metal at just 2.5c/lb. As noted earlier there has been no real improvement in US demand since the end of last year which is reflected in declines in premia. In contrast, Chinese premia have firmed considerably during the month, rising from $60/t in December to $100-120/t at the time of writing. The elevated levels reflect increased demand for LME material because of favourable price arbitrage conditions, given that Chinese prices have been trading above LME quotes since the middle of December. ### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 9000

**Chinese arbitrage opens up once more** Domestic Chinese prices have risen quicker than LME quotes in recent weeks because of continued strong Chinese copper demand, especially from the power sector. In addition, the higher prices are also likely to reflect the standard practice of stockpiling by cathode consumers ahead of the Chinese New Year holiday

which begins on February 14th . The average price arbitrage [SHFE quotes (exclusive of VAT) minus LME prices] narrowed from -$142/t in November to -$8/t in December but then surged to ~+$140/t this month, as of 28th January. As a consequence of the increased in the arbitrage, imports are expected to continue rising into February because of the time lag between when material is booked and is actually delivered. Trade data show that Chinese refined copper imports totalled 244kt in December. This was up by 25.5% month on month and by 15.4% from a year Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2010 Page 3 of 25 Copper Monthly Update earlier. **Chinese demand in 2009 much higher than anticipated** Of all the recent data releases one of the most significant has been Chinese semis production for December. According to the NBS this was 1Mt which represents a 45.6% yearon-year gain and brings last year’s total output to 9.8Mt (+24.9% on 2008). Excluding other alloying metals (~12%) and approximately 10% due to double-counting (e.g. wire rod production in one plant being reported as wire output in another) this means that China’s copper uptake (primary and secondary) into semis is currently around 800kt/m, which is equivalent to an entire year’s copper semis output in a major consuming country such as Italy! The other significant factor about China’s very strong semis production in the closing stages of last year is that this means that proportionately more copper (than was previously thought) has been consumed as opposed to being stockpiled by speculators and others. We estimate that the contribution of scrap to China’s 25% growth in semis output last year was a reduction of 20% (imports were down by 28%) on 2008 meaning that the primary refined component increased by over 30% year on year (SEE CONSUMPTION). For 2010 we do not see anything like a full recovery in scrap availability given the prospects for relatively lacklustre growth in end-use markets within the mature economies. New scrap supplies will be constrained by moderate end use growth in these regions while any surge in the availability of old scrap from the likes of building demolition will require a marked uplift in construction activity which, at present looks unlikely in the US, Europe and Japan. Much of the recent bearish sentiment towards

copper has arisen due to China’s desire to reign in excessive credit growth and the National Grid Company’s decision to reduce its power infrastructure investment by 26% this year. However, very few analysts expect Chinese refined consumption growth to exceed 10% this year, which when compared with 31% in 2009 is dramatically lower. Our 9% Chinese growth figure translates into a global metal market surplus of 150kt. However, if Chinese consumption grows by just over 11% this would put the global market into deficit. With this in mind we feel that the bearish undertone circulating through the market at present may prove to be unfounded. **Sharp fall in market surplus expected this year** As a consequence of our higher Chinese demand figure for last year we now estimate that there was a global market surplus of ~0.9Mt last year compared with 1.2Mt previously anticipated. The LME cash price averaged $5170/t ($2.34c/lb), while metal stocks increased to 66 days of consumption, up from 45 days in 2008. For this year we have raised both our supply and demand forecasts since our December report, and now expect a global market surplus of ~150kt instead of the prior ~270kt. Prices should reflect the more favourable outlook and we now forecast a 2010 average of $7100/t ($3.22/lb). Our increase in refined production from 18.3Mt to 18.6Mt is mainly due to a lower mine disruption allowance, from 6% to 5%. Improved market conditions have led to some mines being reactivated (Freeport’s Morenci Mill) and, possibly others (BHP Billiton’s Pinto Valley?). On the demand side, we forecast a rise in refined copper consumption of 5.9% this year to ~18.5Mt. The driving force behind this recovery is unsurprisingly on account of China. **Demand expected to recover fully in 2011** In 2011 we are forecasting further robust growth in consumption (+6.9%) reflecting a strong recovery in demand outside of China. Supply growth is not expected to keep pace which will result in a market deficit of ~160kt. Metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, will continue to fall throughout the year to just 57 days by year end. Prices, reflecting tighter market conditions, should increase to an average $7225/t ($3.28/lb). Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2010 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Chinese economic growth remained strong through the end of 2009** Coming in ahead of many analysts’ expectations, China’s GDP expanded by 10.7% year on year in Q4 2009, up from 9.1% in Q3, and taking growth for the year to 8.7%. The government’s target had been 8%. Such expansion was driven by unsustainable growth in lending and monetary stimuli, and as these drivers moderate, economic growth likely will move back to a slightly lower trend. The focus is now s

hifting towards the controlling of credit and liquidity, as concerns emerge regarding overheating and dangerous inflationary pressure. **Loan growth surged in 2009** increased to 9.6Tn yuan, equivalent to 32% of GDP and more than double the rate of the previous year. This large increase in lending helped to fuel the 30.5% increase in fixed asset investment in 2009, which has been and continues to be very beneficial for metals demand. The growth in loans had been moderating since its peak in March, due largely to government intervention, but recent developments are likely to trigger an increase in the rate of monetary tightening. Loan growth totalled 380Bn yuan in December, up from 295Bn in November. In addition, state media reported that during the first two weeks of January, new lending reached 1.5Tn yuan, 20% of the 7.5Tn government target for the whole of 2010. This seems to have alarmed China’s authorities, as in reaction they have instructed some major banks to cease lending for the duration of the month, and there have even been unconfirmed reports of some banks being ordered to call back loans already issued. ### **Chinese monthly loan growth (including first two weeks of January 2010)** 2000

**Further constraints to credit likely** The first measure in tightening monetary policy occurred in mid January, as the People’s Bank of China increased reserve requirements for banks; the first time it has changed the reserve ratio since December 2008. The PBoC has also raised the yields on three-month and one-year bills. Generally speaking, the PBoC prints yuan to sell on the foreign exchange markets, with the aim of keeping the exchange rate at its preferred level. By auctioning an equivalent amount of securities, it sterilises the impact of this increased money supply. Early last year sterilisation was partially halted, which was effectively quantitative easing. Raising the yields on its bills increases the demand for them, meaning that a greater number can be auctioned off, thus increasing the rate of sterilisation. This form of quantitative tightening reduces the amount of cash that banks can lend, and appears to be directly aimed at slowing down the increase in net lending from 2009 levels. **Need to balance growth and inflation** The constraints to lending growth will feed through to fixed asset investment, and should result in a slower rate of expansion than was the case at the end of 2009. Industrial production grew by 18.5% year on year in December, down from 19.2% the previous month, and we expect growth to continue to trend lower in the coming months. With exports still recovering, production remains dependent on government stimulus measures. The government is left with a difficult balancing act of avoid

ing dangerous inflationary pressures without damaging the economic recovery. The perils are highlighted in the construction industry, in which activity boomed in 2009, but to which bank lending has been in steady decline since last May (see chart below). Further constraints could severely limit lending in this sector over the next year, reducing the capacity of the private sector to pick up the slack as and when fiscal stimulus measures wane. **Difficult outlook for European industry** Industrial orders for the euro zone point to a slower pace of expansion in the sector in the coming months, as the boost to production from stimulus plans like _Cash for Clunkers_ peters out. The three-month moving average of growth in orders fell to 2.6% in November, from 4.8% the previous month. The data are in line with our view that European manufacturing will expand at a very slow pace in 2010. This view is reinforced by the provisional January PMI for the euro zone, released on January 21, which fell for the first time since last February to 53.6, from 54.2 in December. Industrial orders across the EU have been dragged down by capital goods in particular. With credit conditions remaining tight, and capacity utilisation at just 71.4% in 4Q 2009, compared with ~84% pre-crisis, there is little incentive for manufacturers to invest in new capital during 2010. ### **Capacity utilisation rates in Europe and USA** 90

**USA manufacturing outlook improved** In the USA, the short term outlook continues to improve, although concerns remain about the sustainability of the pace of recovery. The latest PMI data for the US showed that manufacturing expanding at its fastest pace since 2006, consistent with annual GDP growth in the region of 4%. Inventory data for Q4 showed inventories contracting at a much slower pace, indicating that a large inventory boost to manufacturing output should be expected during the first half of 2010, building on the six months of expansion in industrial production that occurred through to December 2009. The concern is how the slack will be picked up once inventory support fades. Capacity utilisation in manufacturing remained at a low 68.8% in December, meaning the need for new capital goods will likely be poor. Furtherm

ore, the outlook for consumption is still bleak. Consequently, we expect to see growth in industrial output slow as we move in the second half of the year. The expansion project cost will be funded out of cash flow and from borrowings by CMA.  Ore reserves at Antamina were increased by approximately 75% in 2008, sufficient to support the expanded operation until 2029. 

**Codelco submits EIS for Chuquicamata underground project** Codelco has submitted an environmental impact statement for the conversion of its mining operation at Chuquicamata from open pit to underground.  The company expects that development will take eight years to complete and is targeting an extraction rate of 140kt/d of ore for the production of 340kt/a of copper in concentrates.  Codelco will spend $34.4M in 2010 on this project or ~2% of the overall projected cost of $1.9Bn.  Capital expenditures on other projects this year include $104.5M on the Andina expansion, $121.9M on the El Teniente expansion and $154.4M on the Alejandro Hales project. 

**Bwana Mkubwa plant reopens to treat Lonshi ore remnants** Following the reopening of the DRC-Zambian border to copper ore exports, First Quantum Minerals (FQM) has restarted its 50kt/a Bwana Mkubwa copper SxEw plant in Zambia.  The plant will process the stockpiled ore from the depleted Lonshi open pit mine.  Production is expected to average approximately 0.8kt/m Cu through to the end of 2010.  In the meantime, FQM continues to seek additional sources of suitable feed including th

e Fishtie deposit in central Zambia. The company has already filed an environmental assessment report with the Environmental Council of Zambia. Identified reserves are apparently sufficient to sustain mining operations for approximately 27 months at a rate of 100kt/m. **Hindustan Copper eyes mine expansions** Hindustan Copper is planning a three-fold increase in ore production over the next five or so years. Prior to the economic crisis the company had been developing the Banwas mine in Rajasthan and the Malanjhand pit in Madhya Pradesh. These two mines currently contribute 2.5Mt/a to Hindustan Copper’s total ore output and once these projects are completed they will add a further 2.5Mt/a. Plans also call for the 19kt/a Ghatsila smelter to be shut down and for the 31kt/a Khetri smelter/refinery to be refurbished and reactivated at a cost of $9M. With Khetri closed during 2009 the company sold 26kdmt of concentrates surplus to Ghatsila’s requirements to Birla. **Finders Resources buys Whim Creek SxEw plant for Indonesian project** Australia’s Straits Resources has sold its 18kt/a Whim Creek SxEw plant to Finders Resources for US$4.4M (paid for with Finder’s shares) with a view to this being used at the latter company’s Wetar project in Indonesia. Dismantling will take 3 months and Finders is aiming to produce 23kt/a Cu. The Wetar copper resource is contained in two separate massive sulphide deposits, Kali Kuning and Lerokis. The combined resource estimate for these two deposits is 9Mt grading 2.4% copper at a 0.5% copper cut off.
